analysis_steps.findings: Across all seven analysis stages, evidence converges on one primary profile defect and two secondary refinements. PRIMARY: Basal insufficiency in 10:00–16:00 afternoon window. Basal 10:00 (0.7 U/h) is 15–25% too low for meal-driven glucose rises; basal 16:00 (0.5 U/h) is 20–30% too low overall (lowest of day during peak-demand afternoon). Glucose averages 148–163 mg/dL (14:00–16:00 local) despite system deploying 3–4 U/h temp basal and SMB every 10 min. Comparable to SMB max ceiling of ~0.22 U per delivery × 6 deliveries/hour ≈ 1.3 U/h SMB, insufficient to cover 40–60 g carbs without basal support. Fix: Raise basal 10:00 to 0.85–0.95 U/h (20–35% increase) and basal 16:00 to 0.7–0.75 U/h (40–50% increase). Testing: Implement one segment at a time (10:00 first, wait 2–3 days, then 16:00); monitor afternoon TIR, TAR, and hypoglycemia risk. SECONDARY 1: Early-morning lows (01:00 local, 18.5% TBR). Root cause is post-evening bolus IOB tail (DIA 10 h, evening boluses 0.2–0.45 U) combined with low basal 00:00 (0.6 U/h). Basal 00:00 appears appropriate for fasting (hour 6–8 post-midnight are excellent, 98% TIR), but at midnight (hour 0, 23:00 local) TBR is 11.4%, and hour 1 (01:00 local, 00:00 UTC on basal 00:00) is 18.5% TBR. Two strategies: (A) Verify basal 00:00 is adequate by observing post-basal-10:00-fix data; if lows persist, reduce basal 00:00 to 0.45–0.55 U/h. (B) Reduce evening boluses slightly (currently 0.2–0.45 U) if start BG <150 mg/dL, or apply temporary target 100 mg/dL (vs. 90) from 22:00–04:00 to suppress SMB correction during recovery from evening bolus. Recommend strategy (A) first (verify basal 00:00 post-basal-10:00-fix); implement (B) only if lows persist. SECONDARY 2: ISF optimization (secondary to basal). ISF 56 mg/dL/U appears overestimated by 15–30% on GLP-1 days (Aug 14+) or in high-glucose states (confidence medium due to no carb logs to validate). Dynamic ISF (70% scaling) is attempting compensation but insufficient. Once basal is corrected and afternoon highs are reduced, residual high-glucose events should decrease in frequency and magnitude; if large highs persist (>200 mg/dL), consider either (1) raising dynamic_isf_adjustment_factor_percent to 85–90% (amplify real-time ISF adjustments), or (2) lowering ISF to 48–52 mg/dL/U (static reduction). Do not change ISF in isolation; must be tested after basal fix. TERTIARY: Meal logging and e-carbs (tertiary to profile). User should log carbs for 3–5 meals to enable (1) validation of CR (is 10.5 g/U accurate for lunch?), (2) verification of ISF effect post-bolus, and (3) context for GLP-1 meals (confirm absorption delay). Once carb logs are available, consider adding e-carbs for GLP-1 meals (estimated 5+ h absorption; e.g., 20 g standard bolus + 30 g e-carbs over 3 h starting 2 h post-meal) to smooth SMB delivery. Prebolus (15 min before meals) should be tested after basal is corrected; currently, reactive bolusing is sufficient given basal deficiency masks prebolus benefit. AUTOMATION: No changes to SMB, UAM, Autosens, or Dynamic ISF indicated. System is functioning correctly and is not the bottleneck. Automation will self-stabilize once basal is corrected. CONFLICT RESOLUTION: CHECKPOINT 1 hypothesized DIA overestimation as a secondary cause of lows; CHECKPOINT 2 noted IOB approaching max (25 U) on high days (Aug 19, 21), suggesting system is protective. However, loop statuses show IOB peaking at 5.9 U (23.7% of max), not saturating. More likely explanation: High IOB on Aug 19, 21 is *symptom* of basal insufficiency (system issuing multiple corrections because basal cannot prevent rises), not *cause* of lows. Once basal is fixed, IOB should return to normal range (2–3 U), and protectiveness will ease. DIA does not need change. CHECKPOINT 3 noted no prebolus and no e-carbs; CHECKPOINT 2 found SMB is adequate for zero-carb-log workflow. Recommendation: Keep meal strategy as-is until basal is corrected and carb logs are available. Prebolus and e-carbs are optimizations, not primary fixes. Confidence is MEDIUM (not high) because GLP-1 confounding (Aug 14+) prevents isolation of basal effect from GLP-1 insulin resistance effect, and lack of carb logs prevents direct CR/ISF/DIA validation.

issues.item: Afternoon hyperglycemia (14:00–17:00 local): sustained elevation 148–163 mg/dL average, peak 162.8 mg/dL at 15:00, 26–32% TAR at peak hours (vs. target 70–90% TIR). Early-morning hypoglycemia (01:00 local): 18.5% TBR (worst hour of day), four severe lows 42–51 mg/dL on Aug 13, 14, 21. Likely cause: post-evening bolus IOB tail (DIA 10 h, evening boluses 0.2–0.45 U at ~18:00–20:00 local) combined with low basal 00:00 (0.6 U/h) at midnight. Subproblem within larger basal context.

ISF (56 mg/dL/U) may be overestimated by 15–30% under GLP-1 or high-glucose conditions; however, confidence is medium because no carb logs prevent isolation of ISF from basal insufficiency. Correction boluses fail to control large highs (e.g., 0.2 U bolus at BG 100 results in BG 177 at 120m post-bolus; could be basal, CR, or ISF defect). Rebound highs after large corrections (2.4 U bolus causing overcorrection 181→94 then rebound 188 mg/dL) suggest either ISF overestimation or DIA underestimation in high-glucose state. Dynamic ISF (70% scaling) is attempting micro-adjustments but insufficient.

GLP-1 context (1.25 mg injections Aug 14, 17, 20) is not reflected in profile. No basal, CR, ISF, or DIA adjustments for GLP-1 presence. Post-Aug-14 data shows slower meal absorption (carbs still rising at 120m in events #10, #13) and higher afternoon TAR (Aug 14, 15, 18, 19 TIR 70.8–83% vs. Aug 8, 9, 16, 17, 20, 21 TIR 88–96%). Boluses are issued reactively (~10–15 min post-meal detection) rather than preemptively. Cannot validate CR (10.5 g/U at 16:00, 13.2 g/U at 08:00) or confirm meal sizes without carb logs.

No extended carbs used (extended_carb_entries=0) despite meal_max_absorption_hours=7 configured and GLP-1-delayed absorption (4–6 h) evident in glucose response patterns. User is not leveraging e-carb feature to smooth slow-absorption meals.

High glycemic variability (COV 32.6%, standard deviation 39.7 mg/dL). Oscillation between afternoon highs (240+ mg/dL) and evening/early-morning lows (41–56 mg/dL) reflects compensation cycles: system corrects high with large bolus, overshoots into low, then corrects low with high temp basal or basal reduction, allowing subsequent rise. GLP-1 context (Aug 14+) causes slow meal absorption (4–6 h); current UAM threshold (8 mg/dL/5 min) may miss early signal on flat GLP-1 meal curves, causing delayed correction. Prebolus is a secondary optimization that becomes more valuable once basal is corrected (reactive bolusing will no longer be necessary as primary coverage). Confidence is LOW because no carb logs prevent direct validation of bolus appropriateness, and GLP-1 effect cannot be separated from meal response patterns.

Undesired outcomes: (1) New lows in 16:00–20:00 evening window (TBR in hour 16–19 increases); (2) Overshooting into low 19:00–22:00 (excessive recovery swing). If desired outcomes, continue. If evening lows appear, reduce basal 16:00 to 0.65 U/h and re-monitor. If afternoon TIR is now >75% but early-morning lows (01:00 local, hour 1) persist or worsen, proceed to step 6.

After 5+ days of basal 10:00 and 16:00 changes stable, review overnight glucose data (23:00–06:00 local). Expected: TBR hour 1 (01:00 local, previously 18.5%) decreases to <10%. If TBR hour 1 is <10%, early-morning lows are resolved; no further action needed. If TBR hour 1 remains >10% or lows recur, proceed to step 7.

implementation_steps.action: Implement contingent basal 00:00 reduction or temporary target strategy.
implementation_steps.details: Option A (Basal 00:00 reduction): Change basal 00:00 from 0.6 U/h to 0.50 U/h (17% reduction). Save and sync. Monitor overnight TBR for 2 days. If lows resolve and no new highs appear overnight, change is confirmed. Option B (Temporary Target strategy): Keep basal 00:00 at 0.6 U/h; instead, set temporary target 100 mg/dL (vs. default 90 mg/dL) from 22:00–04:00 local on days with evening boluses (all days post-basal-fix). This suppresses SMB correction during evening IOB decay, allowing glucose to drift slightly higher overnight while bolus IOB decays, then recovering basal toward target by 06:00. Recommend Option A (basal reduction) first for simplicity; use Option B if Option A causes new hypoglycemia or if user prefers less disruptive approach.

implementation_steps.action: Begin carb logging (parallel with basal monitoring).
implementation_steps.details: Starting immediately: For next 5–7 days, log carbs for representative meals (breakfast, lunch, dinner, and/or snacks). Record: (1) Meal time (local); (2) Carb amount (grams); (3) Composition (standard, high-fat, GLP-1 meal, etc.); (4) Glucose response (capture CGM readings at meal start, +60 min, +120 min, +240 min post-meal). Use AAPS carb entry feature (long-press glucose chart, add carbs) or Nightscout notes (to tag meals). This data will enable CR/ISF validation post-basal-fix.

implementation_steps.action: Assess post-basal-fix response and plan secondary changes (5–7 days post-final-basal-change).
implementation_steps.details: After 5–7 days of basal 10:00, 16:00, and (if applicable) 00:00 changes stable, review overall metrics: (1) Afternoon TIR (10:00–16:00 local): target >75%; (2) Overall TIR: target >88%; (3) TAR overall: target <8%; (4) TBR overall: target <5%. If metrics are met, basal profile is confirmed. If not: (1) If afternoon TIR remains <70% despite basal +20–40%, consider CR or ISF issue (validate with carb logs). (2) If new highs appear (BG >200 mg/dL in previously controlled hours), consider ISF inadequacy (raise dynamic_isf_adjustment_factor_percent to 85–90%, or lower ISF to 48–52 mg/dL/U). (3) If persistent hypoglycemia (TBR >5%), review evening bolus timing and magnitude (may need reduction post-basal-fix) or apply temp target strategy. Document findings and proceed with secondary changes (if any) only one parameter at a time.

implementation_steps.action: Optional: Add prebolus and e-carb strategies (post-confirmation of basal-fix).
implementation_steps.details: Once basal changes are stable and carb logs are available (7+ days): (1) Prebolus strategy: For consistent meals (e.g., daily lunch at 12:00), try prebolusing 15 min before meal (issue bolus at 11:45 for 12:00 meal). Observe whether glucose rise is smoother and bolus magnitude matches CR expectation. (2) E-carbs strategy: For GLP-1 meals (if ongoing) showing slow absorption (>4 h), enter e-carbs in AAPS: standard carbs at meal time, extended carbs starting 2 h post-meal (duration 3 h). Example: 50 g meal → 20 g standard + 30 g extended (starting 120 min, duration 180 min). Observe whether glucose response is flattened and SMB delivery is smoothed. These are refinements; only implement if basal + carb logs support them.

education.topic: Why Basal Profile Matters More Than Bolus
education.content: Basal insulin provides constant background coverage; bolus insulin handles meals and corrections. When basal is insufficient, meals overwhelm the system, requiring large reactive corrections (SMBs and temp basal). This causes oscillation: afternoon high → large correction → evening low → basal recovery → next meal starts high again. Fixing basal (the foundation) stabilizes the system, allowing boluses to be smaller and more predictable. In this case, basal 10:00–16:00 is too low; raising it allows the afternoon meal to be covered proactively, avoiding the high-correction-low cycle.

education.topic: How SMB and Temp Basal Compensate (and Their Limits)
education.content: SMB (Super Microbolus) delivers small insulin doses every 10–15 min in response to glucose rise. Temp basal (temporary basal rate) increases basal delivery to 3–4 U/h on high days. Both are reactive: they respond to deviations from target. System can escalate temp basal to max 12 U/h and deliver SMB up to 0.22 U every 10 min, providing ~1.3 U/h additional coverage. But this ceiling is insufficient if meal carbs require 2–3 U/h basal for 4–6 hours. Basal profile is the primary coverage mechanism; SMB and temp basal supplement it. This analysis shows SMB/temp basal are hitting limits (3–4 U/h deployed on high days), indicating basal insufficiency, not automation failure.

education.topic: GLP-1 Effect on Insulin Sensitivity and Meal Absorption
education.content: GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1) agonists (e.g., semaglutide, dulaglutide) slow gastric emptying, extending meal absorption from 3–4 hours (standard) to 4–6+ hours (GLP-1 meals). They also increase insulin sensitivity (may reduce basal need) or cause insulin resistance depending on dose and formulation. This analysis shows post-GLP-1 injection days (Aug 14, 17, 20) have higher TAR (13–20% vs. 8–10% non-GLP-1 days), suggesting GLP-1 is causing either delayed carb absorption or increased insulin resistance. Profile is not adjusted for GLP-1; carb logs will clarify the effect and inform whether basal/CR/ISF need adjustment on GLP-1 days.

education.topic: ISF (Insulin Sensitivity Factor) and Its Limits
education.content: ISF (56 mg/dL/U in this profile) means 1 unit of insulin lowers glucose 56 mg/dL under fasting conditions. ISF can vary based on meal state (higher with food), time of day (sensitivity varies), activity, and GLP-1 use. When boluses fail to control large highs (e.g., 0.2 U bolus at BG 100 results in BG 177 at 120m), it suggests either (1) ISF is overestimated (insulin is less potent, true ISF ~40–48), or (2) meal carbs are still being absorbed (basal insufficiency). This analysis cannot separate these without carb logs. Carb logging will clarify: if boluses match expected CR-based sizes but glucose still rises, ISF is the issue. If boluses are undersized (system is holding back due to IOB), basal is the issue.

education.topic: DIA (Duration of Insulin Action) and IOB Decay
education.content: DIA (10 h in this profile) defines how long insulin action is assumed to last. IOB (Insulin On Board) is calculated using DIA: bolus IOB = initial_dose × (1 − time_elapsed / DIA). At 10 h DIA, bolus is 50% active at 5 h, 25% active at 7.5 h. If DIA is overestimated, system underestimates IOB decay, causing system to be protective (holding back new corrections) when it shouldn't. If DIA is underestimated, system overestimates IOB decay, allowing stacking of corrections and potential overshoot. This analysis suspects DIA may be slightly overestimated (IOB reaches 4–6 U on high days, system becomes protective), but cannot confirm without basal test or carb absorption curve. Post-basal-fix, IOB should normalize and DIA adequacy will become clearer.

education.topic: Carb Logging and Why It Matters
education.content: Without carb logs, system cannot confirm whether CR (carb ratio) or ISF are accurate, or whether meal sizes are consistent. System infers carbs from glucose rise (UAM), which is approximate. Carb logs (actual measured carb amount + glucose response) allow calculation of true insulin effect: actual_bolus_size / carb_amount = true CR in action. This validates whether 10.5 g/U at 16:00 is accurate, or whether meals are being underestimated. Carb logs also clarify GLP-1 absorption (is meal rise slow because carbs are delayed, or because basal is low?). Recommend 3–5 meals over 7 days, including 1–2 GLP-1 meals if GLP-1 is ongoing.

Prebolus (bolusing 15 min before eating) allows insulin to circulate before carbs arrive, smoothing the glucose response and reducing peak highs. E-carbs (extended carbs) distribute carb coverage over 4–6 hours for slow-absorption meals (high-fat, GLP-1). Both require consistent meal timing/size to be effective. This user is not currently using either; system is reactive (boluses arrive 10–15 min after meal detected). Once basal is corrected and carb logs confirm meal patterns, prebolus and e-carbs become viable optimizations. Prebolus works best if meals are at consistent times (e.g., 12:00 lunch daily). E-carbs work best if GLP-1 meals show consistent slow absorption (4–6 h).

education.topic: How to Recognize When a Change Is Working
education.content: After implementing basal 10:00 change: (1) Afternoon TIR should improve (target >75% in 10:00–16:00 window vs. current ~70%); (2) TAR should decrease (target <15% vs. current 20–32%); (3) SMB frequency should decrease (fewer micro-corrections needed); (4) Temp basal should decrease (system not escalating to 3–4 U/h as aggressively). After basal 16:00 change: (1) Peak afternoon glucose (15:00 local, currently 162.8 mg/dL avg) should decrease toward 140–150 mg/dL; (2) Early-morning lows may improve as evening boluses are smaller. If these do not occur after 2–3 days, basal change may not be sufficient; assess for CR/ISF/DIA defect using carb logs.

safety_notes.note: This is decision-support content only. User must independently verify every proposed change, make changes one at a time, and monitor glucose closely. Do not apply all basal changes simultaneously; implement basal 10:00 first, observe for 2–3 days, then basal 16:00. Rapid simultaneous changes risk unpredictable glucose behavior and hypoglycemia.

Basal changes take 2–4 hours to have full effect (circulation time + insulin onset). Monitor post-change for full day (morning, afternoon, evening) to assess impact. Do not adjust basal multiple times within 24 hours; allow system to reach steady state.

Early-morning lows (01:00 local, currently 18.5% TBR, 4 lows 42–51 mg/dL) are a safety concern. Do not implement basal 00:00 reduction until basal 10:00 and 16:00 changes are confirmed and early-morning TBR has improved post-basal-fix. If new lows appear after basal changes, discontinue and consult care team.

Afternoon highs (240–293 mg/dL on Aug 15, 18) with subsequent large correction boluses (0.45–2.4 U) are a risk for rebound hypoglycemia. Basal increase will reduce reliance on large corrections; monitor for overcorrection (lows in evening/night) as basal decreases afternoon highs.

GLP-1 injections (Aug 14, 17, 20 at 1.25 mg) confound post-Aug-14 data interpretation. If GLP-1 dose is changing (ramping) or if user stops GLP-1, profile will need re-evaluation. Recommend carb logs to quantify GLP-1 effect.

This analysis assumes current profile (dated Aug 21) was in effect for most of Aug 7–21. If profile was changed multiple times during this period, earlier assumptions may not apply. Review AAPS or Nightscout profile history to confirm.

Temporary targets (set 6 times in data) are effective for acute high management; user is leveraging this feature. Recommend continuing selective use (e.g., on GLP-1 days or when lunch is high-carb), but do not rely on temp targets as primary control tool; fix basal instead.

No carb entries recorded throughout 14-day period; system is in zero-carb-log UAM-reactive mode. This is viable but requires accurate UAM threshold (8 mg/dL/5 min) and responsive automation (SMB, temp basal). Once basal is corrected, carb logging will improve predictability and enable further optimization.

Overnight basal (06:00–08:00 local) is excellent (98% TIR, <1% TBR); do not change overnight basal without explicit evidence of a defect. Any overnight changes should be contingent on post-basal-fix monitoring.
Max IOB (25 U) and max basal (12 U/h) are not constraining in this analysis. Do not lower these limits; they are appropriately set for safety. Focus changes on basal profile, not safety ceilings.
